essay.h2Main: Why I built an AI team of twenty-one agents
essay.ledeRest: ive years running marketing for entrepreneurs in Russia — from dental clinics outside Moscow to SaaS founders selling into the US and EU. Two patterns kept showing up that don't go away.
essay.p1: First: the most beautiful sites don't sell. A client comes in with an 80,000-ruble Tilda template that looks like a three-million-ruble brand and asks why nobody calls. Because the site wasn't the task. Selling was. Nobody asked who this is for, what objection it closes, why the headline reads so politely indifferent.
essay.p2: Second: most marketers work on instinct. They don't know Ogilvy's rules, haven't read Schwartz, never opened the Hopkins archive. They write "quality services from a professional team," call it sales copy, and wonder why conversion sits at 0.4%.
essay.pullQuote: Methodology is the contract with the AI. Without rules, ChatGPT writes bland corporate text. With Ogilvy and Schwartz, it sells.
essay.p3: When the serious LLMs arrived — GPT-4, Claude — one thing became clear. AI can do the executional marketer's job ten times faster. But only if you know what to ask for. Walk into ChatGPT with "write me a landing page" and you get bland corporate copy that convinces no one of anything.
essay.p4: I took three libraries of rules that have worked for seventy years. Ogilvy — for headlines and the 80/20 law. Schwartz — for the five awareness levels of the audience. Hopkins — for numbers instead of adjectives. I built 21 specialized AI agents. Each one doesn't just suggest copy. It follows specific rules. The copywriter doesn't write "highest quality" — it writes "92% returned within a year." The positioner doesn't hand you the abstraction "for everyone" — it narrows down to the specific segment where the product actually wins.
essay.p5: This isn't ChatGPT with a system prompt. It's thirty years of marketing discipline encoded into a tool. I'm not selling AI hype. I'm selling a system that works because I didn't invent it. I only assembled it for the marketing market where 80% of agencies and freelancers work on instinct.
essay.p6: If you're reading this and you run a business — your problem isn't the absence of a beautiful site. Your problem is that the site was written by someone who doesn't know the rules. Show this text to whoever did your current marketing and ask: which Schwartz awareness level was the audience on when the hero was written? Which Ogilvy rule is in the headline? Is the bullet number comparable to a benchmark, or is it abstract?
essay.p7: If there's no answer — you know why conversion is 0.4%.
